items.title: @MIT_CSAIL：What if an optimizer could think and react while a neural network trains? MIT researchers developed OPAL: a deep learnin
items.abstract_or_text: What if an optimizer could think and react while a neural network trains? MIT researchers developed OPAL: a deep learning optimizer powered by an AI agent that watches the training dynamics and rewrites its own source code as training goes. It improves model performance across vision and language tasks.

items.title: @rikiyatakehi：We asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to improve math. It directly changed only 0.016% of weights, fixing 0.
items.abstract_or_text: We asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to improve math. It directly changed only 0.016% of weights, fixing 0.8B reasoning loops and improving math up to 6x and even instruction following 3x, without gradients or training. We call this Weight-Space Programming: frontier LLMs can now natively read/write neural network weights.

items.abstract_or_text: I am happy to share FlashProve: our performant open-source prototype for provable inference. We believe that this has significant implications for security, pacing AI development, integrity guarantees, and more. FlashProve allows a provider to commit to model weights, and then prove that replies originate from the committed model. Our library is performant, proving a 400B parameter MoE model at 100 tok/s. We have open-sourced the associated code and Lean formalization.

items.title: @AnthropicAI：We are sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from b
items.abstract_or_text: We are sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life. Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown. With Claude, we have found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery. Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells. For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

Key idea: introduce a hint level, and fit a joint scaling law Accuracy(scale, hint).
